sentences.text: The accused No.1 Neeraj Kumar Nayak was found vending the business of various food articles, including Namkeen which were found stored for sale of human consumption , lying in sealed packets of 400 gms, each bearing identical label declaration.
The food officials lifted the sample the said food article consisting of 3 sealed packets of Namkeen ready for sale.
It was divided into three parts as per procedure prescribed under the PFS Act and Rules and separately packed and sealed.
Necessary documents were prepared at the spot including the vendor's receipt and panchanama.
Price of the sample was paid to the vendor.
One counterpart of the sample was deposited with the public analyst(PA) and remaining two counterparts were deposited with SDM/LHA.

Vide report date 30.07.2009, the PA reported that the article was conforming to the standards, yet the sample was found misbranded being in violation of Rule 24 as best before was declared in a misleadng manner and there was also violation of Rule 32 (2)(a).
Based on the report of PA, investigation was carried out by the Food Inspector as per the instructions of the SDM/LHA.

It was found that Accused No. DA vs Neeraj Kumar Nayak & others 1 Neeraj Kumar Nayak was the vendor of Ms. Spencer's Retail Ltd., 15 Pratap Nagar, Mayur Vihar,
Phase-1, Delhi - 91 at the time of taking the sample.

It is further averred in the complaint that the sampled article of food "Namkeen" was manufactured by M/s Brij Nandan Enterprises and supplied to M/s Spencer's Retail Ltd., accused No.2.

M/s Brij Nandan Enterprises is a proprietorship concern and Accused No.3 Brij Nandan Singh was the proprietor and he looked after its business and such he was incharge of and responsible for day to day conduct of its business.

After obtaining due sanction of the Director, PFA, the present complaint Ex.PW1/E came to be filed against the accused for violation of the section 2(ix)(g)(k) read with Rule 24, Rule 36(2)(a) and Rule 37 r/w Rule 32 (f) & (i) of PFA Rules 1955 as punishable under section 7/16(1)(a) of PFA Act for selling misbranded food.

sentences.text: 8. It is in these circumstances, Ld. SPP for the complainant has argued that the complainant has been able to prove its case against the accused beyond reasonable doubt, as both the witnesses have supported its case and there is no contradiction in their testimony.
It is submitted that the accused persons have failed to rebut the findings as given in the PA Report.

9. On the other hand, Ld. Defence Counsel for the accused No.1 and 2 have argued that accused No.
1 and 2 were only the vendors and the accused No.3 had manufactured and supplied the same and the bill was a part of record.
10. Per contra, it was argued by Ld. LAC for accused No.3 that the complaint was filed after the expiry of shelf life, the right to send the second sample became frustrated.
He also argued that as per the Report of the Food Analyst, the sample lifted was 'Gujarat ka Special Namkeen' and the PA report was of 'Brij Namkeen" which was not the lifted sample items.
He further argued that no intimation or any notice was given to accused No.3 about the Public Analyst report as per the scheme of PFA Act.
11. I have heard the arguments advanced by Ld. SPP for the complaint and Ld. Defence Counsel for the accused and have carefully perused the material available on record.
12. In a criminal trial, the burden is on the complainant / DA vs Neeraj Kumar Nayak & others prosecution to establish its case against the accused beyond reasonable doubt.

entities.text: complainant / DA vs Neeraj Kumar Nayak & others
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: This burden cannot be shifted to the accused and has to be necessarily discharged by the prosecution itself by leading cogent and trustworthy evidence.
13. In the present case, there is no serious dispute as to the steps undertaken by PWs in lifting the sample.
All the PWs, who were a part of the team that had lifted the sample, have deposed in corroboration of each other.
No material contradiction can be seen in their testimony that could go to the root of the matter so as to disbelieve them.
Both deposed about steps undertaken by them during sample proceedings.
Both deposed about compliance of rules while lifting the sample.
No question was put to them regarding non-compliance of any mandatory rule, except putting some general bald suggestions.
Both the witnesses deposed that attempt was made to join public persons as witnesses but none had joined.
There is nothing to disbelieve them or to shake their credibility.
14. The fate of the case depends on quality of witnesses and not their quantity or designation or professions.
There is no rule of law that requires the evidence of food officials to be viewed with any suspicion.
What is required is that attempt is made to join public persons as witnesses as a matter of prudence.
The court is not oblivious of reluctance of public persons to join such legal proceedings that involves lengthy procedural formalities and strict future commitments.

But non joining of such witnesses would not negate the testimony of official witnesses when they are otherwise truthful and Da vs Neeraj Kumar Nayak & Others on 7 May, 2019 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/193241039/

The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Shriram Labhaya v. MCD [1948-1997 FAC (SC) 483] has categorically held that testimony of the Food Inspector alone, if believed, is sufficient to convict the accused and there is no requirement of independent corroboration by public persons unless the testimony suffers from fatal inconsistencies.
No such inconsistency can be seen in this case.
No violation of any rule or provision has been pointed out by the defence.

15. With Respect to Accused No.1 Neeraj Kumar Nayak and Accused No.2 M/s Spencer's Retail Ltd.,
it is seen that accused No.1 Neeraj Kumar Nayak was found admittedly vending the article of food at the time of lifting the sample.
It is also seen the original invoice ExPW2/1 and ExPW1/DX are placed on record.
These bills and invoices have not been denied nor disputed by Accused No.3.
In fact, PW1/DX admittedly contains the signatures of Accused No.3 Brij Nandan Singh, who is the proprietor of M/s Brij Nandan Enterprises.
M/s Brij Nandan Enterprises is the proprietorship concern of accused No. 3 Brij Nandan Singh.

It is also worth mentioning at this stage, the accused No.3 Brij Nandan Singh during his cross examination as DW2 admitted that he had issued the bill Ex. PW1/DX to accused No.2 M/s Spencer Retail Ltd.
Further, it is also requires mentioning that as per Form VI, the sampled product is mentioned as Gujarat ka Special Namkeen.
However in the remaining documents, it is mentioned as Namkeen only.

However, the bill and the purchase order,
both have the same DA vs Neeraj Kumar Nayak & others code number for corresponding items.

sentences.text: Accordingly, it is seen that the sampled food article 'Gujarat ka Namkeen' and 'Namkeen' are referred to the same food items.

Accordingly, it is seen that accused no.3 admitted the factum of the sale commodity and even the original bill of the same is on record, which has not been denied or disputed, Accused No.1 Neeraj Kumar Nayak and Accused No.2 M/s Spencer's Retail Ltd are entitled to the warranty as envisaged u/s 19(2) of PFA Act.
In view of the aforesaid facts, accused No.1 and accused No.2 namely Neeraj Kumar Nayak and M/s Spencer's Retail Ltd. are hereby acquitted in the present.
16. Qua accused No.3 Brij Nandan Singh, it is seen that he has himself admitted that the Ex.PW1/DX belonged to the firm M/s Brij Nandan Singh and was issued by them to M/s Spencer's Retail Ltd.
It is further seen they have taken the defence that the sampled food Article was Gujrat ka Namkeen but other documents have mentioned the food article as Namkeen.
This issue has already been discussed and as already stated that Gujarat ka Namkeen and Namkeen as referred to in the documents pertaining to the sampling refer to one and the same food article.
Another ground of defence as taken by the Ld. LAC for accused No.3 is that they did not receive the intimation and the right u/s 13(2) of PFA Act got frustrated.
It has also been argued that the present complaint was filed after the expiry of the shelf life of the food article.
At the outset, it is worth mentioning that the present case is of misbranding and not of adulteration.

Further, none of the accused persons on entering appearance in this court availed the opportunity to send the counterpart of DA vs Neeraj Kumar Nayak & others sampled food article to Director, CFL for analysis.

sentences.text: Accused No. 3 Brij Nandan Singh examined himself as DW2, he stated that he did not receive the intimation letter.
However, the office copy of the intimation letter Ex.PW1/F, bearing the signature of SDM/LHA and photocopies of the postal registration receipt are collectively Ex PW1/G (OSR).
It has not been stated anywhere by accused No.3 that the address provided in the complaint was wrong and did not belong to him.
Reliance is also placed on the provisions of section 27 of the General Clauses Act which provides that document shall be deemed to serve in the ordinary course of post, unless contrary is proved.
In the present case, nothing has come on record to show that the address of the accused No.3 Brij Nandan Singh was wrong or was incorrect as already discussed.
Therefore, this ground taken by the Accused No.3 also does not hold matter.

sentences.text:
Section 2 (ix) (g) (k) reads as under :-
"misbranded"- an article of food shall be deemed to be misbranded.............if the package containing it, or the label on the package bears any statement, design or device regarding the ingredients or the substances contained therein, which is false or misleading in any material particular .......... if it is labelled in accordance with the requirements of this Act or rules made thereunder.........
Rule 37 provides where the contents are misleading and Rule 32(7) provides for the mention of the month and year in which the commodity was manufactured and Rule 32(i) provides the manner of mentioning the best before date.
18. Perusal of Form VI, Ex.PW2/B shows that the Best Before was declared as Best Before 4 months from Mfg. but date of manufacturing was not mentioned.
The date of packaging was however mentioned as '9 Jul, 2009'.
Therefore, there appears to be no intentional misleading on the part of Accused No. 3 with respect to the aforesaid violations, even if it was not mentioned in the language prescribed.
However, it is pertinent to mention that the label should have mentioned the extraneous addition of colouring matter which was found in the sampled food article which is a clear violation of Rule 24.
Furthermore, the Area of principle display of label was only 18.7% of the size of packet which was not as per the mandated 20% of the size of the packet.
No defence has been lead by accused No.3 that there was no DA vs Neeraj Kumar Nayak & others misbranding on his part of the sampled food article.

entities.text: DA vs Neeraj Kumar Nayak & others
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 19.
